int sum_x(int vx, int tlx, int trx, int lx, int rx, int ly, int ry) {
    if (rx <= tlx || trx <= lx)
        return 0;
    if (lx <= tlx && trx <= rx)
        return sum_y(vx, 1, 0, m, ly, ry);
    int tmx = (tlx + trx) / 2;
    return sum_x(vx*2, tlx, tmx, lx, rx, ly, ry)
         + sum_x(vx*2+1, tmx, trx, lx, rx, ly, ry);
}

This function works in   O(log⁡nlog⁡m)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>log</mi><mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi><mi>log</mi><mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$O(\log n \log m)$  time, since it first descends the tree in the first coordinate, and for each traversed vertex in the tree it makes a query in the corresponding Segment Tree along the second coordinate.

Finally we consider the modification query. We want to learn how to modify the Segment Tree in accordance with the change in the value of some element   a[x][y]=p<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi></math>$a[x][y] = p$ . It is clear, that the changes will occur only in those vertices of the first Segment Tree that cover the coordinate   x<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi></math>$x$  (and such will be   O(log⁡n)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>log</mi><mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$O(\log n)$ ), and for Segment Trees corresponding to them the changes will only occurs at those vertices that covers the coordinate   y<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>y</mi></math>$y$  (and such will be   O(log⁡m)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>log</mi><mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$O(\log m)$ ). Therefore the implementation will be not very different form the one-dimensional case, only now we first descend the first coordinate, and then the second.

void update_y(int vx, int lx, int rx, int vy, int ly, int ry, int x, int y, int new_val) {
    if (ry - ly == 1) {
        if (rx - lx == 1)
            t[vx][vy] = new_val;
        else
            t[vx][vy] = t[vx*2][vy] + t[vx*2+1][vy];
    } else {
        int my = (ly + ry) / 2;
        if (y <= my)
            update_y(vx, lx, rx, vy*2, ly, my, x, y, new_val);
        else
            update_y(vx, lx, rx, vy*2+1, my, ry, x, y, new_val);
        t[vx][vy] = t[vx][vy*2] + t[vx][vy*2+1];
    }
}

void update_x(int vx, int lx, int rx, int x, int y, int new_val) {
    if (rx - lx > 1) {
        int mx = (lx + rx) / 2;
        if (x <= mx)
            update_x(vx*2, lx, mx, x, y, new_val);
        else
            update_x(vx*2+1, mx, rx, x, y, new_val);
    }
    update_y(vx, lx, rx, 1, 0, m, x, y, new_val);
}

Compression of 2D Segment Tree¶

Let the problem be the following: there are   n<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>n</mi></math>$n$  points on the plane given by their coordinates   (xi,yi)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$(x_i, y_i)$  and queries of the form "count the number of points lying in the rectangle   ((x1,y1),(x2,y2))<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$((x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2))$ ". It is clear that in the case of such a problem it becomes unreasonably wasteful to construct a two-dimensional Segment Tree with   O(n2)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$O(n^2)$  elements. Most on this memory will be wasted, since each single point can only get into   O(log⁡n)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>log</mi><mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$O(\log n)$  segments of the tree along the first coordinate, and therefore the total "useful" size of all tree segments on the second coordinate is   O(nlog⁡n)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mi>log</mi><mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$O(n \log n)$ .

So we proceed as follows: at each vertex of the Segment Tree with respect to the first coordinate we store a Segment Tree constructed only by those second coordinates that occur in the current segment of the first coordinates. In other words, when constructing a Segment Tree inside some vertex with index   vx<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>v</mi><mi>x</mi></math>$vx$  and the boundaries   tlx<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>t</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>x</mi></math>$tlx$  and   trx<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>x</mi></math>$trx$ , we only consider those points that fall into this interval   x∈[tlx,trx]<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>t</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></math>$x \in [tlx, trx]$ , and build a Segment Tree just using them.

Thus we will achieve that each Segment Tree on the second coordinate will occupy exactly as much memory as it should. As a result, the total amount of memory will decrease to   O(nlog⁡n)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mi>log</mi><mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$O(n \log n)$ . We still can answer the queries in   O(log2⁡n)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>log</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$O(\log^2 n)$  time, we just have to make a binary search on the second coordinate, but this will not worsen the complexity.

But modification queries will be impossible with this structure: in fact if a new point appears, we have to add a new element in the middle of some Segment Tree along the second coordinate, which cannot be effectively done.

In conclusion we note that the two-dimensional Segment Tree contracted in the described way becomes practically equivalent to the modification of the one-dimensional Segment Tree (see Saving the entire subarrays in each vertex). In particular the two-dimensional Segment Tree is just a special case of storing a subarray in each vertex of the tree. It follows, that if you gave to abandon a two-dimensional Segment Tree due to the impossibility of executing a query, it makes sense to try to replace the nested Segment Tree with some more powerful data structure, for example a Cartesian tree.

Preserving the history of its values (Persistent Segment Tree)¶

A persistent data structure is a data structure that remembers it previous state for each modification. This allows to access any version of this data structure that interest us and execute a query on it.

Segment Tree is a data structure that can be turned into a persistent data structure efficiently (both in time and memory consumption). We want to avoid copying the complete tree before each modification, and we don't want to loose the   O(log⁡n)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>log</mi><mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$O(\log n)$  time behavior for answering range queries.

In fact, any change request in the Segment Tree leads to a change in the data of only   O(log⁡n)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>log</mi><mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$O(\log n)$  vertices along the path starting from the root. So if we store the Segment Tree using pointers (i.e. a vertex stores pointers to the left and the right child vertices), then when performing the modification query, we simply need to create new vertices instead of changing the available vertices. Vertices that are not affected by the modification query can still be used by pointing the pointers to the old vertices. Thus for a modification query   O(log⁡n)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>log</mi><mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$O(\log n)$  new vertices will be created, including a new root vertex of the Segment Tree, and the entire previous version of the tree rooted at the old root vertex will remain unchanged.

Let's give an example implementation for the simplest Segment Tree: when there is only a query asking for sums, and modification queries of single elements. 

struct Vertex {
    Vertex *l, *r;
    int sum;

    Vertex(int val) : l(nullptr), r(nullptr), sum(val) {}
    Vertex(Vertex *l, Vertex *r) : l(l), r(r), sum(0) {
        if (l) sum += l->sum;
        if (r) sum += r->sum;
    }
};

Vertex* build(int a[], int tl, int tr) {
    if (tr - tl == 1)
        return new Vertex(a[tl]);
    int tm = (tl + tr) / 2;
    return new Vertex(build(a, tl, tm), build(a, tm, tr));
}

int get_sum(Vertex* v, int tl, int tr, int l, int r) {
    if (r <= tl || tr <= l)
        return 0;
    if (l <= tl && tr <= r)
        return v->sum;
    int tm = (tl + tr) / 2;
    return get_sum(v->l, tl, tm, l, r)
         + get_sum(v->r, tm, tr, l, r);
}

Vertex* update(Vertex* v, int tl, int tr, int pos, int new_val) {
    if (tr - tl == 1)
        return new Vertex(new_val);
    int tm = (tl + tr) / 2;
    if (pos < tm)
        return new Vertex(update(v->l, tl, tm, pos, new_val), v->r);
    else
        return new Vertex(v->l, update(v->r, tm, tr, pos, new_val));
}

For each modification of the Segment Tree we will receive a new root vertex. To quickly jump between two different versions of the Segment Tree, we need to store this roots in an array. To use a specific version of the Segment Tree we simply call the query using the appropriate root vertex.

With the approach described above almost any Segment Tree can be turned into a persistent data structure.

Finding the   k<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>k</mi></math>$k$ -th smallest number in a range¶

This time we have to answer queries of the form "What is the   k<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>k</mi></math>$k$ -th smallest element in the range   a[l…r)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>…</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$a[l \dots r)$ . This query can be answered using a binary search and a Merge Sort Tree, but the time complexity for a single query would be   O(log3⁡n)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>log</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$O(\log^3 n)$ . We will accomplish the same task using a persistent Segment Tree in   O(log⁡n)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>log</mi><mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$O(\log n)$ .

First we will discuss a solution for a simpler problem: We will only consider arrays in which the elements are bound by   0≤a[i]<n<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>n</mi></math>$0 \le a[i] \lt n$ . And we only want to find the   k<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>k</mi></math>$k$ -th smallest element in some prefix of the array   a<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi></math>$a$ . It will be very easy to extent the developed ideas later for not restricted arrays and not restricted range queries. Note that we will be using 1 based indexing for   a<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi></math>$a$ .

We will use a Segment Tree that counts all appearing numbers, i.e. in the Segment Tree we will store the histogram of the array. So the leaf vertices will store how often the values   0<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>0</mn></math>$0$ ,   1<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>1</mn></math>$1$ ,   …<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>…</mo></math>$\dots$ ,   n−1<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></math>$n-1$  will appear in the array, and the other vertices store how many numbers in some range are in the array. In other words we create a regular Segment Tree with sum queries over the histogram of the array. But instead of creating all   n<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>n</mi></math>$n$  Segment Trees for every possible prefix, we will create one persistent one, that will contain the same information. We will start with an empty Segment Tree (all counts will be   0<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>0</mn></math>$0$ ) pointed to by   root0<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>r</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>$root_0$ , and add the elements   a[1]<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></math>$a[1]$ ,   a[2]<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></math>$a[2]$ ,   …<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>…</mo></math>$\dots$ ,   a[n]<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></math>$a[n]$  one after another. For each modification we will receive a new root vertex, let's call   rooti<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>r</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>$root_i$  the root of the Segment Tree after inserting the first   i<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>i</mi></math>$i$  elements of the array   a<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi></math>$a$ . The Segment Tree rooted at   rooti<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>r</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>$root_i$  will contain the histogram of the prefix   a[1…i]<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>…</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></math>$a[1 \dots i]$ . Using this Segment Tree we can find in   O(log⁡n)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>log</mi><mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$O(\log n)$  time the position of the   k<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>k</mi></math>$k$ -th element using the same technique discussed in Counting the number of zeros, searching for the   k<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>k</mi></math>$k$ -th zero.

Now to the not-restricted version of the problem.

First for the restriction on the queries: Instead of only performing these queries over a prefix of   a<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi></math>$a$ , we want to use any arbitrary segments   a[l…r)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>…</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$a[l \dots r)$ . Here we need a Segment Tree that represents the histogram of the elements in the range   a[l…r)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>…</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$a[l \dots r)$ . It is easy to see that such a Segment Tree is just the difference between the Segment Tree rooted at   rootr<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>r</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub></math>$root_{r}$  and the Segment Tree rooted at   rootl−1<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>r</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"><mi>l</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>$root_{l-1}$ , i.e. every vertex in the   [l…r)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>…</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$[l \dots r)$  Segment Tree can be computed with the vertex of the   rootr<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>r</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub></math>$root_{r}$  tree minus the vertex of the   rootl−1<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>r</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"><mi>l</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>$root_{l-1}$  tree.

In the implementation of the   find_kth<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mtext>find_kth</mtext></math>$\text{find_kth}$  function this can be handled by passing two vertex pointer and computing the count/sum of the current segment as difference of the two counts/sums of the vertices.

Here are the modified   build<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mtext>build</mtext></math>$\text{build}$ ,   update<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mtext>update</mtext></math>$\text{update}$  and   find_kth<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mtext>find_kth</mtext></math>$\text{find_kth}$  functions

Vertex* build(int tl, int tr) {
    if (tr - tl == 1)
        return new Vertex(0);
    int tm = (tl + tr) / 2;
    return new Vertex(build(tl, tm), build(tm, tr));
}

Vertex* update(Vertex* v, int tl, int tr, int pos) {
    if (tr - tl == 1)
        return new Vertex(v->sum+1);
    int tm = (tl + tr) / 2;
    if (pos < tm)
        return new Vertex(update(v->l, tl, tm, pos), v->r);
    else
        return new Vertex(v->l, update(v->r, tm, tr, pos));
}

int find_kth(Vertex* vl, Vertex *vr, int tl, int tr, int k) {
    if (tr - tl == 1)
        return tl;
    int tm = (tl + tr) / 2, left_count = vr->l->sum - vl->l->sum;
    if (left_count >= k)
        return find_kth(vl->l, vr->l, tl, tm, k);
    return find_kth(vl->r, vr->r, tm, tr, k-left_count);
}

As already written above, we need to store the root of the initial Segment Tree, and also all the roots after each update. Here is the code for building a persistent Segment Tree over an vector a with elements in the range [0, MAX_VALUE].

int tl = 0, tr = MAX_VALUE + 1;
std::vector<Vertex*> roots;
roots.push_back(build(tl, tr));
for (int i = 0; i < a.size(); i++) {
    roots.push_back(update(roots.back(), tl, tr, a[i]));
}

// find the 5th smallest number from the subarray [a[2], a[3], ..., a[19]]
int result = find_kth(roots[2], roots[20], tl, tr, 5);

Now to the restrictions on the array elements: We can actually transform any array to such an array by index compression. The smallest element in the array will gets assigned the value 0, the second smallest the value 1, and so forth. It is easy to generate lookup tables (e.g. using   map<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mtext>map</mtext></math>$\text{map}$ ), that convert a value to its index and vice versa in   O(log⁡n)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>log</mi><mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$O(\log n)$  time.

Dynamic segment tree¶

(Called so because its shape is dynamic and the nodes are usually dynamically allocated. Also known as implicit segment tree or sparse segment tree.)

Previously, we considered cases when we have the ability to build the original segment tree. But what to do if the original size is filled with some default element, but its size does not allow you to completely build up to it in advance?

We can solve this problem by creating a segment tree lazily (incrementally). Initially, we will create only the root, and we will create the other vertices only when we need them. In this case, we will use the implementation on pointers(before going to the vertex children, check whether they are created, and if not, create them). Each query has still only the complexity   O(log⁡n)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>log</mi><mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$O(\log n)$ , which is small enough for most use-cases (e.g.   log2⁡109≈30<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>log</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>9</mn></msup><mo>≈</mo><mn>30</mn></math>$\log_2 10^9 \approx 30$ ).

In this implementation we have two queries, adding a value to a position (initially all values are   0<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>0</mn></math>$0$ ), and computing the sum of all values in a range. Vertex(0, n) will be the root vertex of the implicit tree.

struct Vertex {
    int left, right;
    int sum = 0;
    Vertex *left_child = nullptr, *right_child = nullptr;

    Vertex(int lb, int rb) {
        left = lb;
        right = rb;
    }

    void extend() {
        if (!left_child && left + 1 < right) {
            int t = (left + right) / 2;
            left_child = new Vertex(left, t);
            right_child = new Vertex(t, right);
        }
    }

    void add(int k, int x) {
        extend();
        sum += x;
        if (left_child) {
            if (k < left_child->right)
                left_child->add(k, x);
            else
                right_child->add(k, x);
        }
    }

    int get_sum(int lq, int rq) {
        if (lq <= left && right <= rq)
            return sum;
        if (max(left, lq) >= min(right, rq))
            return 0;
        extend();
        return left_child->get_sum(lq, rq) + right_child->get_sum(lq, rq);
    }
};

Obviously this idea can be extended in lots of different ways. E.g. by adding support for range updates via lazy propagation.
